Text｜Sleepy

Johor Bahru has no mountains.

Johor Bahru is the capital of Johor, the southernmost state in Malaysia, separated from Singapore only by the Johor Strait. The highest point in the city is just a small hill, called Bukit Timbalan in Malay, and Flag Hill by the older Chinese. On the hill stands the Sultan Ibrahim Building, completed in 1940, which was formerly the Johor state government. In early 1942, the Japanese army used it as their command post for the attack on Singapore. Standing on the building and looking south, across the strait is Woodlands, the northernmost point of Singapore, with rows of government-built public housing blocks standing on the shore.

Even the name "Johor Bahru" was brought from the other side. In the Kranji area in northwestern Singapore, gambier was once widely planted. The branches and leaves of this shrub were boiled down to make a paste that could be used for tanning leather and dyeing cloth.

The older generation of Chinese called that place "Old Mountain." Later, the land ran out of nutrients, and the firewood for making oil palm oil was all cut down. So people crossed the strait and settled in Johor, which became known as Johor Bahru. One hundred and eighty years later, Old Mountain was once again completely depleted. In 2019, Singapore suspended approvals for new data centers, as land, fresh water, and electricity resources reached their limits. So people crossed the sea again. [Image of YTL Green Data Center Park entrance in Kulai, Johor | Source: Paul Mah] The two small towns of Kulai and Senai, located 30 kilometers north of Johor Bahru, where oil palm oil was once made along the riverbank, now house server rooms. Solar panels have been laid on over 1,600 acres of converted oil palm land, and the server room buildings are taller than the surrounding oil palm trees. In just over three years, Johor's data center capacity has surged from 10 megawatts to 1.3 gigawatts. According to a 2026 report by real estate consultancy Knight Frank, Johor's planned data center pipeline reaches 8,542 megawatts, ranking first in the Asia-Pacific region. The Senai Technology Park has now been incorporated into a new development area of ​​over 7,000 acres, named Ibrahim Technology City, after the Sultan of Johor, Ibrahim. At the park's opening, the president of Johor's state government investment agency explained the division of labor to the media: Johor provides land and scale, while Singapore provides capital and speed. Water is rarely absent from the naming conventions of Southeast Asian Chinese. Over a hundred years ago, those who carried silver dollars and letters back to their ancestral homes in China for Southeast Asian Chinese were called "water carriers." Singaporean water carriers typically traveled south in December with the northeast monsoon and returned north in June of the following year with the southwest monsoon. In the early years, they took a 10-20% commission, which later decreased to 3% as more people entered the trade. They didn't draw up written agreements or seek guarantors; they relied on shared hometowns and clansmanship, knowing which village your family lived in. The recipient would send a short message as a reply, often written by the smugglers. Later, the term "smuggler" specifically referred to those who carried goods across the Shenzhen River between Shenzhen and Hong Kong. For example, at the Hong Kong port of the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge, a private car declared as empty was stopped; its trunk contained approximately 280 kilograms of live lobsters, with 70 old professional graphics cards underneath. However, in the eyes of those in the computing power business in Singapore and Malaysia, the graphics card resale business across the Shenzhen River was just small-scale. The truly large-scale operators used a Singaporean entity to directly buy cards from upstream suppliers, transported the machines to data centers in Malaysia, used several layers of intermediary companies, and then leased the computing power to large Chinese manufacturers. According to them, for a long time, this wasn't even considered smuggling because it was legal. In February 2025, Nvidia listed Singapore separately in its financial reports for the first time. That fiscal year, revenue with invoicing addresses in Singapore amounted to $23.684 billion, accounting for 18% of total revenue; by the end of July, this proportion had risen to 22%. This city-state of over six million people once supported more than one-fifth of the chip giant's revenue. On the same page, in small print, Nvidia noted that while customers used Singapore for centralized invoicing, products were almost always shipped elsewhere; goods actually delivered to Singapore accounted for less than 2% of revenue that fiscal year. In November 2025, Nvidia switched to disclosing revenue based on customer headquarters location, and the Singapore entry disappeared from its financial reports. As for Malaysia, just across the strait, it never appeared in Nvidia's financial reports during those years. Until November 13, 2026, the Malaysian Ministry of International Trade and Industry reiterated that no permits were required to import AI chips into Malaysia; only exports and transshipments required them. Three days later, the U.S. Department of Commerce issued new regulations requiring licenses for the export of advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil. Only end users headquartered in the U.S. could switch to monthly reporting. Similarly, any data center worldwide providing large-scale computing power to companies headquartered in China would also require a license. Within days, Dark Side of the Moon canceled a $150 million contract to lease Nvidia B300 chips through Indonesia. To secure the chips, the company had agreed to prepay half the cost, whereas industry practice is only 15%. Just two months prior, ByteDance had secured a $29.6 billion syndicated loan from multiple banks, with Chinese banks subscribing to over 60%. Sources revealed that this money was primarily invested in overseas AI infrastructure. Those in this business view this tightening as a campaign-style enforcement measure. During crackdowns, everyone shrinks back, and once the heat dies down, they can add more layers of intermediaries between Chinese customers and data centers, allowing business to continue. Like in Yoshiki Tanaka's *Legend of the Galactic Heroes*, the Galactic Empire and the Free Planets Alliance fought for over a century, with the Fraser Dominion sandwiched in between. While openly locked in a life-or-death struggle, their under-the-table dealings never ceased, requiring a tacitly agreed-upon place to facilitate their transactions. Singapore, at its core, is a Chinese society, yet outwardly maintains a distance from China; Malaysia, at its core, is an Islamic country, yet outwardly maintains close ties with China. These two countries happen to have the highest proportion of overseas Chinese in their populations. The narrowest point of the strait is less than a kilometer. The Tebrau River harbor deed. Around 1824, on a Saturday morning at five o'clock, Abdullah, a Malacca resident, left Singapore with five Chinese men. He was the Malay clerk for Raffles, a British colonial official and the founder of Singapore; later known as Wensi Abdullah, "Wensi" meaning teacher in Malay.

A Gambier and Pepper Plantation in Singapore around 1900 | Image source: National Museum of Singapore

That day he wore tattered trousers, an old cloth draped over his shoulders, a tattered handkerchief wrapped around his head, and carried a one-rupee copper coin, a small knife, a pencil, and a piece of paper in his pocket. The guide was a secret society leader, a Malay-speaking Chinese man born and raised in Malacca, locally known as "Baba."

The group avoided the official roads, taking shortcuts, crossing tree stumps, traversing swamps, and wading through muddy water. Baba told him that if the road were easy, the police, soldiers, and Europeans would have arrived long ago. When they were almost there, Baba had Abdullah take the bundle and umbrella, pretending to be a Malay beggar they had encountered on the road, instructing him to just play dumb.

At noon, they rested at a jasmine garden. The people there served him cucumbers and roasted sweet potatoes. He ate under the shade of a tree, secretly counting the weapons on the wall: large shields, iron tridents, long and short swords, and a row of muskets leaning against the wall. At four o'clock in the afternoon, they arrived at a settlement deep in the forest. Before them were three large huts, the longest over fifty meters. Moats were dug around them, and drawbridges were set up at the entrances. Only those who knew the residents would lower the drawbridges; beyond the drawbridges were ditch pits covered with turf. Lamps were lit inside the huts, and the walls were piled with sharpened wooden stakes and bamboo poles. There were about five or six hundred people inside, less than twenty of whom did not smoke opium. At nightfall, the drums were beaten. Abdullah was ushered into the secretary's small room with a curtain, peeking out through the gap in the curtain. Five or six hundred people ate, drank, and made a ruckus for an hour, the noise like a battle. Then music started, and the crowd sat in rows facing the idol, their faces flushed red with intoxication. The leader sat on a high chair, with eight swordsmen standing on either side, their swords drawn. A disheveled, shirtless newcomer was brought in, forced to kowtow, and two swords were simultaneously placed against his neck. The leader asked him who his parents were, whether they were alive or dead. Even if his parents were still alive, the newcomer had to answer, "My parents are both dead." Joining the order was tantamount to dying for the mortal world. A vessel was placed in front of the idol, filled with Yala, a strong spirit from Southeast Asia brewed with coconut juice and rice, mixed with the blood of the members. The newcomer pricked his finger with a sword, dripped his blood into the wine, took a small sip, and then the leader and hundreds of members passed it around in turn. After the ceremony, the leader instructed him to find the scribe the next day to obtain a booklet printed with the rules and secret codes. Next, a man with his hands tied behind his back was brought in. He refused to kneel and was struck more than a dozen times with a bamboo stick. When asked if he wanted to join the society, he remained silent. A knife-wielder made a move to strike him, but the leader raised his hand to stop him. When asked again, he still refused. The leader said, "Execute him tomorrow morning." What Abdullah saw through the curtain that night was what the 19th-century Chinese in Southeast Asia called a "company." In those days in Southeast Asia, this term could refer to a garden jointly owned by several people from the same hometown, or it could refer to an armed secret society that worshipped gods and swore oaths. The Heaven and Earth Society was a secret society that originated in Fujian and Guangdong during the Qing Dynasty; the Chinese in Singapore and Johor called it the "Yi Hing Company." A company had its own incense hall, laws, and thugs, as well as its own cemetery. The company's business originally grew in a gambier garden. Boiling gambier consumed a lot of firewood, and the rainforest surrounding the garden was cut down piece by piece, forcing the owner to move deeper into the forest. By 1844, Singapore's forests were nearly depleted. Across the strait in Johor, Temenggong Daim Ibrahim, a powerful royal minister, possessed vast tracts of uncultivated forest but lacked both manpower and funds. He began issuing Malay documents called Surat Sungai to Chinese leaders, which the Chinese called "harbor deeds." Those who received a harbor deed could cultivate land along a designated river, becoming the harbor's owner. Each river was essentially a small, independent kingdom. That year, Chen Kaishun, a 41-year-old Teochew man, reportedly led four thousand Yixing brothers across the strait, traveling along the Tebrau River, now located in the eastern suburbs of Johor. They built Chen Cuo Harbor, named after his surname, on the riverbank, which at its peak housed five thousand people. The river teemed with crocodiles, and the forests with tigers, so they erected a statue of Tua Pek Kong, a local deity worshipped by the Chinese in Southeast Asia, on the riverbank to ward off evil. On May 5, 1854, at noon, a Fujianese man and a Teochew man in Singapore got into an argument over a pound of rice. Fellow countrymen from both sides lined up, and hundreds surged into the streets. Shops were bolted, and sticks, stones, and knives flew through the air. The governor, riding a white horse, entered the town to quell the unrest, but was driven back by the mob, who didn't recognize him. By dawn on the third day, several hundred more people had entered the town, all brought in overnight by secret society leaders from the jungles and sailing ships in the harbor. In those ten days, four or five hundred people died, three hundred houses burned, Singapore's trade came to a standstill, grain ships couldn't cross the strait, and the laborers along the Johor River immediately ran out of food. The Malay rulers of Johor knew exactly how to use this force to generate wealth. In 1873, Johor enacted the Harbour Master Act, consisting of eighty-one articles. Article 2 stipulates that the port lord receives two rattan canes and a spear as symbols of authority; Article 11 allows the port lord to establish a private court, detaining prisoners for no more than three days, administering no more than six lashes, and imposing fines of no more than ten dollars; Article 75 is the crux of the entire law, granting the port lord a monopoly on opium and alcohol within his jurisdiction, monopolizing the pork trade, and the right to operate gambling dens and pawnshops. The kingdom's capital came from Singapore. A typical Johor Gambier company was often composed of several growers with the same surname plus a Singaporean boss who provided the capital. In Hokkien, such a boss is called a "headman," who would extend credit to the growers at four to six times the market price. The port contracts themselves were split and resold between the two sides. The fuel that kept this machine running day and night was opium. Singapore's opium factories lit fires at three in the morning every day to boil raw opium imported from India into a black paste. The leftover residue, called "opium dregs," was sold cheaply to the poor; the ash left after smoking the dregs could be sold again. The rich used silver pipes with ivory tips, while laborers lay on high bunks in the opium dens, using silver needles to pick out the opium by lamplight. A pack of cheap opium sold for forty cents, just enough to cover half a day's work for the laborer. Wages, paid by the landlord, passed through the opium den counter and flowed into the hands of conglomerates that monopolized the sales, eventually becoming taxes paid to the colonial government and the Johor royal family. These sales were essentially the government leasing the monopoly on opium and alcohol to merchants; the highest bidder won, and the merchants paid monthly rent, keeping the rest for themselves. Between 1825 and 1910, in the Straits Settlements of Singapore, Penang, and Malacca, which were under British control, opium revenue consistently accounted for 30% to 50% of the government's annual income, reaching as high as 59% in 1904. The monthly rent for opium and alcohol services in Temenggong skyrocketed from 350 dollars in 1847 to 8,000 dollars in 1860. Most laborers toiled their entire lives for nothing; opium consumed about two-thirds of their wages, binding them to their employers' debts. From 1870 to 1879, Fujianese merchant Zhang Fanglin, Teochew merchant Chen Chengbao, and Chen Xunian, the largest port owner in Johor, joined forces to monopolize opium and alcohol services in Singapore, Johor, Malacca, and the Riau Islands south of Singapore—a scheme British merchants called the "Great Syndicate." In 1876, Zhang Fanglin funded the transformation of a vacant lot in front of the police court into Fanglin Park. By 2000, it had been designated Singapore's "Speakers' Corner," becoming the only place in the country where citizens could publicly give speeches and hold assemblies without needing a police permit. Coolies were continuously transported by sea. In 19th-century Singapore, it was the labor exchange for the entire Southeast Asia. Around 50,000 people arrived annually in the 1870s, rising to 200,000 around 1900. Penniless people would "buy on credit," their tickets unpaid until the ship docked, then locked in the hold, waiting for a mine owner's or plantation owner's comprador to redeem their tickets before they were taken away like livestock. In South China, this business was called "selling piglets." Chen Xunnian, who monopolized the contracts for four ports, is said to have also entered the seas in this way. Born in Jinshazhai, Haiyang County, Chaozhou, he lost his father at a young age and sold oil. In 1853, he obtained his first port deed, and ten years later, he acquired four ports in a single week, naming the largest one after his hometown's common name, Shalong Port. In 1870, he was appointed head of the Johor Chinese community, a position unprecedented and unparalleled. That same year, he began construction of the Congxi Ancestral Hall in his hometown of Chaozhou, a project that took fourteen years to complete and cost approximately 260,000 silver dollars. In 1875, Chen Xu Nian suddenly sold off all his properties in Johor and returned to Singapore overnight; the reason remains a mystery. The year before Chen Xu Nian left Johor, in the tin mining region of Perak on the west coast of the Malay Peninsula, the two major political parties, Yi Xing and Hai San, were locked in a bitter struggle for control of the mine's waterways. A gambling dispute led Hai San to arrest fourteen Yi Xing members and kill thirteen. With the tin supply cut off, the British finally found a pretext to enter the market. On January 20, 1874, the colonial steamship Pluto was anchored off Pangkor Island in the Perak Sea. The Governor of the Straits Settlements signed a treaty with Perak Malay nobles aboard. Britain would send a resident official, and all government affairs, except those concerning religion and Malay customs, would be subject to his advice. Twenty-six Chinese were also present on board, led by the heads of the Yi Hing and Hai San families. From then on, Narut changed his name to "Taiping." Hai San leader Zheng Jinggui later became Perak's largest tin mine owner, donating 100,000 taels of silver to the Qing government in exchange for a second-rank official position. In 1893, he bought the former headquarters of the Penang Yi Hing Company and converted it into his own grand mansion, which is now the Penang Peranakan Museum. The Gambling Game of Kampung Ah Fook Around the time of the brawl over a kilogram of rice in 1854, a 17-year-old man from Taishan, Guangdong, arrived in Singapore by sailboat. His name was Huang Yafu, and he was from Yanjing Village in Taishan. Unable to pay his boat fare, he sold himself to a carpenter to pay off a debt. After a year of hardship, he stayed on and, a few years later, received a share of the carpenter's shop. In 1863, he built two warehouses for Temenggong's agent in Singapore, which is how he met the future Sultan of Johor, Abu Bakar. In the decades that followed, he built the Johor palace, as well as the prison and seawall in Johor Bahru. In December 1892, the Sultan's Istana Tesser in Singapore was completed, also built by him; it is said to be the first building in Singapore to be electrified. The Sultan's reward to him was a charter. In September 1892, Abu Bakar granted Huang Ya Fu a 99-year lease on a plot of land in Johor Bahru, with a nominal annual rent of only S$120. The first right listed in the original Malay document was permission to operate a casino on the land. In Malay, a village is called a "kampung," and that plot of land later became known as Kampung Ya Fu. This was during the era when Johor Bahru served as a casino for Singapore. Singapore had banned gambling as early as 1829, but Johor did not. In 1903, the railway between Singapore and Woodlands opened, and gamblers disembarked and transferred to the Singapore or Johor ferries to cross the sea. Sundays were the busiest days, and people compared Johor Bahru to the Monte Carlo of the East. Casino owners generously paid for gamblers' train tickets back to Singapore on Sundays, and the third-class carriages were always packed on Sunday nights. Huang Ya Fu's casino operated under the very nose of the Sultan of Johor, and also during Singaporeans' weekends, inevitably attracting envy. In 1908, another gambling contractor wrote a letter complaining about unfair competition in Kampung Ah Fook. The Sultan immediately ordered that no outsiders be allowed to gamble, and the police simply stationed themselves at the entrance of the gambling den to block them. The two sides later reached an agreement: one would pay the government 1,000 ringgit per month, and the police would withdraw. However, on New Year's Day 1915, the police returned to the gambling den. Huang Ah Fook filed a lawsuit against the Johor state government. On August 7, 1915, the Johor High Court ruled in favor of Huang Ah Fook. The judge cited the constitutional declaration signed by the Sultan himself in 1908, stating that a person who rules by personal will rather than by law is not a true ruler; the Sultan is also under the law, and the court has the right to review the Sultan's orders. Three years later, Huang Ah Fook died at his home in Singapore. Today, there is still a Huang Ah Fook Street in downtown Johor Bahru. Huang Ah Fook's generation slowly came ashore on the old planks of secret societies and gambling dens. In 1890, Singapore banned secret societies, and in 1909, it brought opium under state control. Johor was a step behind, ordering the dissolution of the Ghee Hing in 1916 and abolishing the port authority system by the end of the following year. In 1955, Singapore enacted the Criminal Code (Temporary Provisions) Ordinance, and three years later added the power to detain secret society members without trial, citing fear of retaliation among witnesses. This provisional law is renewed every five years, with the most recent renewal starting in October 2024. Now, its list of targets includes loan sharks; in 2019, the authorities used this law to detain the head and financier of a loan sharking group involved in over 1,800 cases of harassing debtors. The old secret societies have disbanded, but the network of kinship and clan ties remains, only now with a more respectable shell. The first shell to emerge is the bank. In 1903, Huang Yafu, together with several fellow Cantonese, established Kwong Yik Bank, Singapore's first Chinese bank. Its predecessor was actually an internal money exchange where Huang Yafu printed his own money on his plantation to pay wages and then collected workers' savings. What truly solidified the Chinese banking industry was rubber. Singapore was formerly known as "Singapore," and the Straits Settlements currency was in use at the time. The price of rubber plummeted from 1.14 Singapore dollars per pound in 1925 to a mere 4 cents during the Great Depression of 1932. The three banks—Ho Fong, Hua Shang, and Hua Qiao—merged to form today's OCBC Bank. Lee Kong Chian, who spearheaded the merger, was the son-in-law of rubber tycoon Tan Kah Kee. Three years later, Huang Qingchang, whose ancestral home was Kinmen, opened UOB Bank in a three-story building on the banks of the Singapore River, specializing in business with Fujianese merchants. The Chong Kio Bank, later acquired by UOB, was founded by Hu Wenhu, a Hakka who made his fortune with Tiger Balm and the Sin Chew Daily. In 1937, Aw Boon Haw built Haw Par Villa in Singapore and personally supervised the creation of clay sculptures of the Ten Kings of Hell, with the Fourth King specifically responsible for punishing tax evasion and commercial fraud. However, on the Malay Peninsula, it wasn't so easy for the Chinese to settle down safely. In June 1948, Malaya declared a state of emergency, and the British colonial government aimed to suppress the Malayan Communist Party, which had retreated into the mountains to wage guerrilla warfare. The British discovered that the guerrillas relied entirely on the Chinese scattered along the forest edges for rice, medicine, and intelligence. From 1950 onwards, approximately 500,000 people, mostly Chinese, were surrounded by police and military trucks before dawn. They were taken away with their entire families before they could even pack their belongings, and confined to 450 "new villages" surrounded by barbed wire. Robert Kuok, born in Johor Bahru, a native of Fuzhou, studied at Raffles Institution in Singapore, where he was classmates with Lee Kuan Yew. During the Japanese occupation, he worked as a clerk in Mitsubishi Rice and Grain Department. After the war, he and his brothers founded the Kuok Brothers Company, which at one point monopolized 80% of the sugar market in Malaysia, making him known as the "Sugar King of Asia." His younger brother, Kuok Hock Ling, joined the Malayan Communist Party and died in the jungle during the state of emergency. On May 13, 1969, racial violence erupted in Kuala Lumpur. Two years later, the New Economic Policy, aimed at supporting the economic status of Malays, was introduced, forcibly requiring companies to relinquish shares to Malays and other indigenous groups. In his memoirs, Kuok wrote that his shipping company was twice asked to issue more shares to Malay institutions, who told him it was merely the price of his success. Since status was valuable, some people simply bought it. "Datuk" is an honorary title in Malaysia, similar to a knighthood in the UK, awarded by the Sultans, Governors, or the Yang di-Pertuan Agong (King) of Malaysia, who rotate among the nine hereditary Sultans. According to AFP, between 700 and 1,200 new Datuks are appointed annually, leading some politicians to jokingly remark that "you could throw a stone on the street and hit a Datuk." In 2023, the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) dismantled a syndicate selling titles. On the black market, a Datuk sold for RM150,000, a higher-ranking Datuk Seri for RM250,000, and a Tan Sri for RM2 million. Only the Sultan of Johor, Ibrahim, refused to sell. He publicly stated that an intermediary offered RM2 million for one of his assigned Tan Sri positions. In 2026, for the Sultan's birthday, Johor will only award four Datuks, all of whom are police officers or civil servants. In other states, however, the title is often associated with illicit businesses. In 2021, the Pahang state palace revoked businessman Liao Shunxi's Dato' Seri title after police discovered his syndicate was involved in transnational fraud and had at least 34 law enforcement officers on their payroll. Some people have also found a different path to success. Lin Wutong, a native of Anxi, Fujian, went to Southeast Asia at the age of 19 to work as a carpenter. In 1965, he worked on a road in Ulu Kali, northeast of Kuala Lumpur. Originally planned to take 15 years to build, he overcame 180 landslides and completed the road in three years, creating what is now Genting Highlands. On April 28, 1969, Genting received Malaysia's first and only casino license. According to Genting, the application process took only six hours from submission to approval. Today, the pathways to success are wider and quieter. In Singapore, there were only about 400 family offices established by wealthy families specifically to manage their own wealth at the end of 2020, but this number is expected to exceed 2,000 by the end of 2024. Penang Chinese businessman Jho Low took a different shortcut. In June 2009, he opened an account at a private bank in Singapore for a Seychelles shell company, and $700 million from Malaysia's sovereign wealth fund, 1MDB, immediately flowed into the account in Zurich. The US Department of Justice estimates that Jho Low and his accomplices misappropriated more than $4.5 billion from this fund. This money was used to purchase a Beverly Hills mansion, paintings by Monet and Warhol, investments in "The Wolf of Wall Street," and a 92-meter-long giant yacht with two helipads. In 2016, the Monetary Authority of Singapore revoked the commercial banking license of Swiss bank BSI in Singapore for this reason, the first time since 1984. On the evening of November 10, 2026, 73-year-old former Prime Minister Najib Razak returned to his home in Kuala Lumpur under police escort, receiving a pardon and being placed on home duty. Jho Low remains missing, while the yacht seized by the Malaysian government was sold to Genting Group for US$126 million back in 2019. Myawaddy and Phnom Penh The 19th-century Ghee Hin Company needed a rainforest colonizers wouldn't bother with, and a harbor deed issued by the Temenggong; the 21st-century underwater companies need the same thing: an enclave beyond the reach of state power, a local warlord or noble willing to pay for protection, and a blood vessel leading to China. Along the fragmented borders of Southeast Asia, such enclaves are strung together. In the Golden Triangle bordering Thailand, Myanmar, and Laos, Zhao Wei, a timber merchant from Northeast China, leased 10,000 hectares of land along the Mekong River from the Lao government in 2007 for a 99-year term. Clocks in the special economic zone run on Beijing time, the currency is RMB, and Chinese signs are everywhere. Hundreds of kilometers to the west lies Kokang in northern Myanmar. After 2009, the four major families, including Bai Suocheng, grew powerful with the support of the Myanmar military, controlling administration, militia, police, and hundreds of closed gambling and fraud zones. The 41 zones controlled or jointly owned by the Bai family alone involved gambling and fraud exceeding 29 billion RMB. By the end of 2023, the four major Kokang families were destroyed amidst gunfire, and by 2026, their core members had been executed. But while Kokang collapsed, the small town of Myawaddy, separated from Thailand by the river on the Thai-Myanmar border, still exists. Here, the word from the 19th-century Singapore Chinatown Coolie Museum has been revived intact. Those lured into the parks are collectively called "piglets," and each piglet is worth between 100,000 and 200,000 yuan, depending on their education and typing speed.

KK Park on the banks of the Moai River on the Thai-Myanmar border | Image source: Jittrapon Kaicome

Where does the money earned from these parks ultimately go?

Sources told Beating that although many of the operators of these parks are based in Myanmar and Cambodia, the major shareholders who hold board meetings according to the articles of association and receive the lion's share of profits have long since laundered their money and are now living in Kuala Lumpur.

On March 15, 2020, the "Investor Appreciation Gala" of the Myawaddy East Mey Industrial Park was openly held at the Marriott Hotel in Kuala Lumpur. Wan Kuok-koi, the former leader of the Macau 14K triad known as "Broken Tooth Koi," who was instrumental in promoting the park, also became the chairman of a Malaysian listed company that same year. In Cambodia, the owners of fraudulent and gambling operations are called "operation owners" in the industry, and they don't even need to maintain private armies. Just like buying a Datuk in Malaysia, they directly buy "nobility" in Cambodia. The Cambodian government confers nobility titles on major donors, raising the threshold from US$100,000 to US$500,000. The number of people conferred nobility titles has more than doubled; 631 people were conferred titles between 1955 and 2016, while 711 people will be conferred titles in just nine years from 2017 to 2025. Chen Zhi of the Prince Group is one of them. Born in Lianjiang, Fuzhou in 1987, he made his first fortune running an internet cafe and setting up private game servers in his hometown. He became a Cambodian citizen in 2014, and four years later, he bought a Cypriot passport. In 2020, he was granted the title of High Noble, became an advisor to former Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Sen, and also opened his own Prince Bank. In October 2025, the US Department of Justice indicted Chen Zhi and filed a civil lawsuit to seize approximately 127,000 Bitcoins. Two months later, Cambodia swiftly stripped him of his citizenship and title. On January 6, 2026, Chen Zhi was arrested in Phnom Penh and the following day was put on a flight to Beijing. One hundred and fifty years ago, money flowed northward in this sea area. The laborers, having earned their hard-earned money along the Johor River, after deducting tobacco expenses and interest from their employers, would stuff the remaining change into remittance slips and entrust them to sea carriers traveling north with the monsoon winds. These slips would then be delivered to ancestral halls and families in Chaoshan and Southern Fujian months later. Later, as the sea carriers' business expanded, specialized remittance agencies emerged to handle remittances and messages for overseas Chinese. Even when the British colonial government forcibly established a government post office in Singapore in 1876, sparking a bloody riot among Chaozhou merchants, and even after the outbreak of the Pacific War and the subsequent fall of Singapore and Hong Kong, and the Japanese blockade of sea routes, these private remittance agencies could still detour through the jungle trails of Mong Cai in Vietnam and Dongxing in Guangxi to send money back to their homeland. Now, the waterways have reversed. Money flowing from China and graphics cards flowing from the United States are meeting head-on at this crossroads of Southeast Asia.

Some of the designer handbags seized by Singapore police | Image source: Singapore Police Force

Some of the money flowing south is dirty. In the jargon of the black and gray industries, the money deposited by victims and gamblers is called "material". The "gambling material" lost by gamblers is the cleanest, rarely reported to the police, and has the lowest commission for laundering; while the money obtained by impersonating public security, procuratorate and law enforcement is the hottest, and has the highest commission. The gangs responsible for collecting and withdrawing the money using domestic bank cards and then exchanging it into USDT, a stablecoin pegged to the US dollar, are called "caravans", and the dens that specialize in laundering it are called "water rooms".

In the 19th century, smugglers relied on kinship and hometown connections to establish trust, but today's caravans and operators in the jungle of black market operations trust no one.

As a result, a number of escrow platforms sprang up on Telegram. The teams would first deposit USDT on the platform, which would then create a group chat containing the buyer, seller, and escrow agent to manage the funds. Only after confirming the money was safely and securely received would the loan be disbursed. The largest of these was Huiwang Guarantee, owned by the Cambodian Huiwang Group. From its launch in 2021 until its ban in May 2025, Huiwang Guarantee handled over $31 billion in transactions, and its subsidiary, Huiwang Payment, had a transaction volume of at least $103 billion, earning it the nickname "Southeast Asia's Alipay." Another platform specializing in Chinese-language business, "Singapore Coin Guarantee," registered in Colorado, USA, was banned by Telegram. It then migrated its merchants to an encrypted chat application developed by a Singaporean company. On September 9, 2026, the US Treasury Department designated it a transnational criminal organization, freezing over $52 million in assets. Singapore Coin Guarantee immediately announced a switch to a different stablecoin to continue operating. As blockchain analytics firm Elliptic stated, the financial network in this area is merely migrating, not collapsing. The laundered fortune eventually needs to find the safest place to be stored. On August 15, 2023, Singapore deployed over 400 police officers in a province-wide operation, arresting ten Chinese nationals simultaneously in sprawling detached houses in Bukit Timah, a long-established affluent area in central Singapore, and in luxury homes on Pearl Island in Sentosa Cove. None of the ten were Singapore citizens or permanent residents, but they carried passports from various countries, including China, Cambodia, Cyprus, Vanuatu, Turkey, Saint Kitts and Nevis, and Dominica. Police seized boxes of gold bars, hundreds of designer handbags, hundreds of luxury watches, thousands of bottles of fine wine, a grand piano, and 56 Bearbricks. The seized assets ballooned from S$1 billion initially reported to over S$3 billion. The Singapore government spent S$2.65 million over two years just on renting storage facilities for these stolen goods. In July 2026, Deloitte was commissioned to auction 47 luxury cars, including at least 11 Rolls-Royces. One of the Rolls-Royces, a Phantom, had been parked in a warehouse for nearly three years, with a total odometer reading of only 284 kilometers. All ten defendants pleaded guilty and received sentences ranging from 13 to 17 months. After serving their sentences, most were deported to Cambodia. Su Binghai, who escaped the raid, was driven across the Johor Causeway by an employee on the night of the raid and calmly flew away from Kuala Lumpur International Airport two days later. International investigative journalists later discovered that just seven days after fleeing Singapore, a company under Su Binghai's name bought nine apartments near Buckingham Palace in London; in late 2024, he spent £12.4 million at a London auction to purchase three Jurassic dinosaur skeletons. Singaporean authorities issued fines totaling over S$27 million to nine financial institutions, including Credit Suisse, UBS Singapore, and UOB Singapore. However, a former industry insider told Beating that Singapore has always been fully aware of the origins of this money. It simply needed to attract various forms of speculative capital in its early years. Now, Singapore's economy has far surpassed Hong Kong's, and with its coffers full, it naturally has the right to choose its clients. Meanwhile, the supporting services beneath the surface have never ceased. In early 2021, Xie Yong, a Singapore company secretary, held nominal positions as a director in 980 local companies, managing shell companies for Chinese clients. Some of the nominal directors he recruited charged only 50 Singapore dollars per name. When the Inland Revenue Board of Malaysia investigated the shadow economy in 2026, it found that about 90% of the companies involved were held by locals on behalf of others, and among the nominal major shareholders were even homeless people on the streets. About 70 kilometers off the east coast of Johor, there is an anchorage of 1200 square kilometers, roughly the size of Hong Kong. It lies precisely between Malaysia's territorial waters and its exclusive economic zone. In this area, coastal states can control the resources within the waters, but not the ships that pass through. It's marked on nautical charts as the "Eastern Outer Harbour Boundary." On any given day, hundreds of giant ships float on its surface, and maritime consultants estimate that nearly half of them are linked to Iran. In late July 2026, an Iranian oil tanker, HUMANITY, 330 meters long—equivalent to placing the Eiffel Tower horizontally across the sea—passed through the Singapore Strait. Its Automatic Identification System (AIS), broadcasting its location, was disabled at the Malaysian outer customs checkpoint, and it completely disappeared from radar screens. During that month, a total of 18 Iranian-flagged oil tankers sailed to this area and then vanished without a trace.

Malaysia seizes two oil tankers during transshipment | Image source: Malaysian Maritime Enforcement Agency

Transshipment is the jargon for transferring oil to another ship at sea. In late January 2026, two sanctioned oil tankers were caught transshipping oil off Penang. One of the tankers was carrying $129 million worth of crude oil. As a result, both ships were allowed to set sail after paying a $76,000 deposit, the maximum penalty under Malaysian maritime law. The fine amounted to only 0.06% of the cargo's value. The giant tanker carrying crude oil slowly rounded Singapore and anchored off Johor.

On this sea, even the land itself has been renamed and transported.

When Singapore gained independence in 1965, its land area was 581.5 square kilometers. By mid-2025, it had expanded to 736.3 square kilometers. The extra 155 square kilometers were mostly created by filling in land with sand from neighboring countries. Malaysia banned sand imports in 1997, and Indonesia banned sea sand in 2002. Exporters then changed the description of sea sand to "land sand" on customs declarations. More than twenty small islands in the Riau Islands south of Singapore have been dredged from nautical charts by sand dredgers. In October 2024, the Indonesian Minister of Fisheries, while inspecting Batam, the largest island in the Riau Islands closest to Singapore, intercepted a 130-meter-long sand dredger in the open sea. The crew, including 13 Chinese nationals, were on deck, and the hold was filled with tens of thousands of cubic meters of sea sand dredged up over nine hours. The captain insisted the sand was dredged from off the coast of Muar in western Johor and was destined for Changi in eastern Singapore. A month later, unable to prove whether the sand in the hold belonged to Indonesia or Malaysia, the Indonesian authorities had no choice but to let the ship go. Crude oil and sea sand change their origins at sea, while AI chips change their names in warehouses on shore. In Texas, some businessmen removed the original labels from Nvidia H100 and H200 chips, affixed their own fabricated brand SANDKYAN, and declared them as ordinary computer parts. In Florida, a real estate company called Janford Realtor, which hadn't sold a single house, smuggled 400 A100 chips into China via Malaysia and Thailand in just a few months. In March 2026, the US Department of Justice indicted the co-founder of a major server manufacturer, widely believed by the media to be Supermicro. The indictment stated that a Southeast Asian company placed $2.5 billion in server orders over two years. The defendant had prepared thousands of counterfeit servers that couldn't even be turned on. When auditors inspected the premises, the counterfeit servers were neatly stacked in the warehouse, while the genuine machines had already been shipped to China. In the free trade zone of Kuala Lumpur International Airport, 72 and 30 servers fully loaded with AI chips were intercepted by customs in June and October 2026, respectively. The customs declarations listed them as computer parts and electronic parts, respectively. These disguised chips ultimately ended up in data centers in Johor. Data centers consume a lot of electricity and water. Singapore's history of drawing water from Johor predates its purchase of sand. A water supply agreement signed in 1962 remains in effect, allowing Singapore to draw up to 250 million gallons of raw water daily from the Johor River at a fixed price of RM0.03 per thousand gallons—a price that has remained unchanged for over sixty years. The water pipeline crosses the strait along the Johor Causeway. Today, the river upstream of this old pipeline simultaneously feeds residents on both banks, sand quarries, and an ever-growing density of data centers. In late October 2025, a sand washing pond at a sand quarry in Kota Tinggi, southeastern Johor, breached, releasing muddy slurry into the Johor River. The raw water turbidity reading skyrocketed from a normal 400 to 37,400, an increase of more than ninety times. All water treatment plants along the river, including those operated by Singapore Water in Johor, were shut down, leaving 800,000 people without water, and more than a ton of dead fish floated on the river. In November 2026, the Johor State Assembly revealed that 19 operating data centers across the state had originally requested 73.08 million liters of water per day, but the state government only approved less than one-third of that. In Gelang Patah, on the western outskirts of Johor, a large section of a hill called Bukit Resam was cleared to make way for a 43-hectare data center park. Krishnan, an aircraft engineer living 400 meters from the construction site, had to buy two new air conditioners and keep the doors and windows tightly closed to ensure his family could sleep peacefully away from the noise and dust. On February 7, 2026, he led more than 50 neighbors to block the construction site gate, launching the first anti-data center protest in Malaysian history. The developer's appeasement plan was to lay 10,000 square meters of dust-proof netting and provide free car washes for nearby residents. The 1056-meter-long causeway... Mornings in Johor Bahru begin at 4 a.m. The motorcycle lights at the checkpoint form a long red dragon, slowly moving towards the other side of the strait. Every day, 300,000 to 400,000 Malaysians cross the strait to work in Singapore like migratory birds. On peak days, the two land border crossings between Malaysia and Singapore handle nearly 589,000 people.

The Johor Causeway as seen from Johor Bahru to Singapore | Image source: CNA

Of the two checkpoints, the older one is on the Johor Causeway. This causeway, built in 1924, connects Johor Bahru and Woodlands, and is actually only 1056 meters long.

When it's blocked, impatient people simply abandon their cars and walk. On a Friday night in January 2025, during a monsoon rain, someone braved the rain and walked along the edge of the road for 36 minutes to cross the border; in July, a Johor bus drivers' strike left thousands of workers with no choice but to walk across the causeway.

A businessman who travels between Singapore and Malaysia told Beating that the scene is strikingly similar to the route taken by illegal immigrants trekking across Central America to enter the United States. Heavy trucks roar past all around, and almost every year, night travelers lose their lives on the causeway.

On weekends, the flow of people reverses. Over a century ago, Singaporeans took Sunday trains and ferries across the strait to Kampung Afar to gamble; now they drive in to fill up with cheap petrol, get massages, and empty supermarket shelves. In the first seven months of 2025 alone, over 11 million people flocked to the area. On the eastern side of the causeway, the cross-border MRT connecting Johor Bahru and Woodlands has been completed. Once operational in early 2027, the crossing will only take five minutes. Further west along the coast, on four artificially reclaimed islands at the western entrance to the strait, stands Forest City, a new maritime city jointly developed by Chinese developer Country Garden and a local Johor partner. This new city, which was touted as housing 700,000 people, has a 30-40% stake held by the local partner, whose controlling shareholder is the Sultan of Johor. From mid-2025 to mid-2026, only 13 homes were sold in Forest City. Warning signs reading "Beware of Crocodiles, No Swimming" stand on the beach, and a lone yacht is moored on the shore. In July 2026, Johor police arrested 335 telecom fraud suspects on the island, 309 of whom were Chinese nationals who had only been transferred from Cambodia to the island a few weeks prior. The same island was also once home to utopian believers from Silicon Valley. Former Coinbase CTO Balaji rented space on the island to establish a Network School. In July 2026, the city hall revoked his license, and the very next day, Balaji signed a memorandum of understanding with Kazakhstan. Previously, there were rumors that Forest City would rely on issuing casino licenses to revive its economy. The Chief Minister of Johor, who heads the state government, specifically refuted these rumors on Facebook, stating that Johor had closed casinos since the time of the late Sultan Ibrahim, and the current Sultan would never allow Johor to reopen casinos. The deceased Sultan mentioned by the minister was the same one who sent police to guard the entrance of Wong Ah Fook's casino a century ago; the current Sultan, Ibrahim, is his great-grandson. This Johor Bahru resident is also the Yang di-Pertuan Agong (King) of Malaysia, owning approximately 300 luxury cars, including a 1936 Mercedes-Benz 540 that is said to have been a gift from Hitler to his great-grandfather. He also commands the Johor Royal Army, the only state-owned private army in Malaysia owned by the royal family. In 2010, he obtained his train driver's license, and the following year, the Malayan Railway departed from Tanjong Pagar, the terminus of Singapore, on its last train journey. It was this very Sultan himself who sat in the driver's cab, driving the train back to Johor Bahru. On the waters of the Strait, relics of the old era are being dismantled bit by bit. For example, the stilted wooden houses built by fishermen in the shallow sea for fishing and fish farming, which locals call "Kwailong." The last few remaining kelong (traditional Singaporean kilong) in Singapore are being demolished, with the maritime department setting a deadline of December 31, 2026 for clearing them out. However, every year on the 21st day of the first lunar month, the procession of deities in Johor Bahru's old town continues past midnight. The Johor Ancient Temple, an old temple for the Chinese community in Johor Bahru, enshrines five deities representing five dialect groups: Teochew, Hokkien, Hakka, Cantonese, and Hainanese. Every year during the first lunar month, the temple parades the deities' statues through the streets. On the evening of March 9, 2026, at 7:20 PM, the night procession began, with over ninety floats leading the way, and tens of thousands of devotees surrounding the palanquin, walking eight kilometers around the city before arriving at the main stage on Jalan Wong Ah Fook two hours later. Among the crowd was a 41-year-old French R&D manager who personally carried a section of the palanquin. As the procession began, devotees chanted in unison in Teochew and Hokkien, "Prosper! Thrive!" Older residents of Johor Bahru remember that this century-old procession had its share of times when even the palanquin bearers couldn't afford to carry it. After the decline of Gambier and Pepper in the early 20th century, fewer and fewer young Chinese were willing to help carry the palanquin, forcing the temple to hire poor people and Indians to do so. Later, a story circulated in the city that a poor young man had turned his luck around and made a fortune by carrying the palanquin for the temple. From then on, the number of Chinese eager to carry the palanquin increased year by year. On the Mian Yu Ting Cemetery, a public cemetery for Chinese in Johor Bahru, there is a solitary grave built in 1921 called "Ming Tomb." In 1916, the Yi Xing Company was ordered to dissolve by the Johor government. After liquidation, the remaining 20,000 ringgit was awarded by the court to Foon Yew School, founded by Chinese in Johor Bahru, with a condition attached: Foon Yew must send someone to Ming Tomb to pay respects every year. The elders say that there are actually no skeletons buried under the Ming tomb; it only contains the ancestral tablets of the Yi Xing Company. Today, Foon Yew High School is one of the largest independent Chinese secondary schools in Malaysia, with three campuses and over 14,000 teachers and students. Its board of directors, composed of leaders from five different gangs, still visits the tomb containing the gang's tablets twice a year, in spring and autumn, to pay their respects. 180 years ago, Chen Kai Shun led 4,000 Yi Xing brothers across the sea to develop Johor Bahru. After his death, he was buried in a rubber plantation in Chen Chu Kang. Later, the rubber plantation was sold to a real estate developer, and the old port lord's grave could no longer be found. However, his ancestral tablet was later retrieved from the Huangpu River in Singapore across the strait. Now, some people involved in chip smuggling are already looking for their next destination. Some have set their sights on Canada, where there is a large Chinese population, it is close to the United States, and the cold weather makes server room cooling cheaper. The only drawback is the high cost of labor.

On November 20th, Bitcoin closed at $58,851, a pullback of approximately 53% from its October 2025 high.

Several commonly used cyclical indicators are giving conflicting signals: the original rainbow chart has been broken below the model by the price, the "500 days before the halving" rule points to a window around November 30th, while the MVRV, which measures the total cost of holding Bitcoin across the network, remains above 1.

On November 20th, Bitcoin closed at $58,851, a pullback of approximately 53% from its October 2025 high.

Several commonly used cyclical indicators are giving conflicting signals: the original rainbow chart has been broken below the model by the price, the window pointed to by the "500 days before the halving" rule is around November 30th, and the MVRV, which measures the total cost of holding Bitcoin across the network, remains above 1.

... This article, based on daily and on-chain data since 2010, lists the performance of eight commonly used cyclical indicators at various tops and bottoms. Readers can also re-fit the rainbow chart themselves.

Panorama: Aligning the four cycles by halving day, the peak times almost overlap, and the gains narrow in each cycle

If we uniformly denote the prices on the halving days of 2012, 2016, 2020, and 2024 as 1, and overlay the four trends on the same chart: the latter three bull markets all peaked between 525 and 546 days after the halving, with a time difference of no more than three weeks; however, the maximum gain after the halving decreased from 92 times to 1.9 times.

Note: The vertical axis uses a logarithmic scale. The 2012 cycle peaked on the 371st day after the halving, about five months earlier than the subsequent three cycles, making it the only exception; while the 2024 cycle reached a new historical high a month before the halving (March 2024), something that did not occur in the previous three cycles.

Note: The vertical axis uses a logarithmic scale.

Each row in the table below corresponds to one indicator. The left side records the tops of four bull markets, and the right side tracks the subsequent bear market bottoms. Starting from the lowest point of the previous bear market, the peaks of the four bull markets are 539 times, 112 times, 21 times, and 7.9 times its previous value, respectively, and the annualized volatility also decreases from 98% to 45%. Frequently Asked Questions

Can the Bitcoin Rainbow Chart still be used as a reference?

The original rainbow chart from 2014 was breached by the price twice, in 2022 and 2026. Based on the old curve, today's center price was estimated at approximately $1.09 million, while the actual price was only around $60,000. The maintainer himself stated that it is not a predictive tool. Although the refitted version places the current price in the lower band, the fact that it needs to be refitted itself indicates that the old curve is no longer applicable.

Why didn't the Pi Cycle Top trigger in 2025?

Why didn't the Pi Cycle Top trigger in 2025?

This indicator requires the 111-day moving average to cross above twice the 350-day moving average, provided that the price of the coin rises sharply within a few months. In the previous three bull markets, the peak ratio of these two lines reached 1.23, 1.06, and 1.00 respectively, while in this round it only reached a high of 0.74. Slower price increases mean the short-term moving average cannot catch up with twice the long-term moving average. What does it mean if MVRV falls below 1? What is the current reading? MVRV equals the circulating market capitalization divided by the total cost of holding coins across the entire network. A reading below 1 means that all holders on the network are, on average, in a state of unrealized loss. At the bottoms of the bear markets in 2015, 2018, and 2022, this indicator fell to 0.56, 0.69, and 0.75 respectively; as of November 22, 2026, the reading was 1.15, and the lowest it has reached so far in this round is only 1.10. What is the basis for the "buy 500 days before the halving" rule? This is an empirical rule promoted by analyst Crypto Rover, advocating buying approximately 500 days before the halving and selling approximately 500 days after the halving. Based on daily closing price backtesting, the bottoms of the first three bear markets occurred 542, 513, and 528 days before the next halving, while the peaks of the latter three occurred 525, 546, and 534 days after the halving. The next halving is expected around April 13, 2028, which, counting back 500 days, is November 30, 2026. However, there are only three to four historical samples. Can these indicators be used alone to determine buying and selling opportunities? They cannot be used as the sole basis for decision-making. The data review in this article shows that the cyclical patterns in the time dimension still conform to historical data, while the fixed thresholds in the amplitude dimension are becoming increasingly difficult to reach, and none of them were triggered in this round. Furthermore, the conclusions of the bottom-fishing indicators are inconsistent.

Data and Definitions

Price, MVRV, market capitalization, and miner revenue are all taken from daily data published by the Coin Metrics community, covering the period from July 18, 2010 to November 22, 2026. Because the daily closing reference price is used, the high point recorded in 2025 was $124,824 on October 6, slightly lower than the intraday peak of approximately $126,000 often cited by the media; the lowest closing price so far in this round is $58,525 on June 30, 2026.

data.title: How to value crypto projects?
data.description:
1. Can you analyze MSTR?

This company is often talked about. I looked at it a long time ago, but I didn't understand it.

My evaluation standard for this company is the same as for other companies: I look at the discounted value of its total future free cash flow.

By this standard, I don't understand how its operation can generate a continuous and stable free cash flow in the future.

There is a similar company, BMNR.

However, BMNR allows users to use their accumulated ETH to participate in staking mining and receive 2% to 3% staking income annually.

Even so, I don't understand how BMNR's cash flow (in USD terms) can be stable in the future.

Therefore, I basically don't look at these kinds of companies now.

2. Do you use group chats to improve your understanding?

I don't use this method to improve my understanding.

Even in groups, I basically don't participate in the chat.

Most conversations end in a pointless debate where neither side can convince the other. People's opinions are difficult to change, so arguing about opinions is pointless; it's a waste of time and energy and leads to internal conflict. I mainly learn methods and lessons from experience by reading books; I mainly acquire information and search for news online. 3. How do you value projects in the cryptocurrency space? Many projects only have a roadmap when they launch. Valuing a project and having only a roadmap are not contradictory; they are two separate issues. I divide crypto projects into three categories: The first category generates no cash flow; the second category generates cash flow; and the third category combines both. Bitcoin and some NFTs belong to the first category. This category is difficult to value; it relies entirely on personal intuition and experience, and there is no unified standard, so I won't elaborate here. Ethereum, in my opinion, belongs to the third category. Its attributes are complex, with many factors contributing to its value. It generates cash flow: on one hand, ETH can be used for staking to generate staking income; on the other hand, the entire Ethereum platform collects transaction fees from applications. It has buybacks for "shareholders" and "stocks": using the Ethereum network requires burning ETH. It provides security: serving all applications and services running on it, services that theoretically offer returns and should be priced. However, it's difficult to quantify the value generated by these services using current methods. Additionally, it has a value storage function, which is also difficult to quantify. Therefore, this type of asset is not easy to value. I'm currently using cash flow for valuation, and then considering other value-generating factors based on intuition and experience. UNI, AAVE, etc., belong to the second category in my opinion. I believe this type is valued based on cash flow. I think valuing this type of project is not too difficult. The biggest problem with these types of projects isn't how to value them, but how their valuation can be truly reflected in the tokens—that is, whether the project has token buybacks (burns) or "cash" dividends to token holders. As for the comments mentioning that some projects only have roadmaps, I don't think that affects the valuation. The key is whether you can extract the elements that influence the valuation from the roadmap, such as the business model and corporate culture. First, determine which of the three asset categories it belongs to based on its business model, and then choose the appropriate valuation method for each category. After having a valuation method, then assess whether the team can actually implement and launch its business model based on the corporate culture—I guess this is what the comments are most worried about. How can you believe that a project can be launched if many teams have no background? If you can see this, you can roughly calculate the valuation. If not, the operation is simple—just ignore it. For projects that only have a roadmap and result in losses for participants, I think the biggest problem isn't whether the project can be valued, but that participants haven't actually valued it at all. Instead, they blindly believe in the project's "vision" and think it has "value."
